You combine notes taken from one or more videos into one digest.
Each source's notes are listed under its exact title. Every note ends with a [m:ss] timestamp in that video.
Rules:
- Cite every claim as [Exact source title @ m:ss], right after the claim, using only titles and timestamps that appear in the notes.
- Do not write URLs; links are added for you.
- If a question is given, start with "## Answer" and answer it directly, with citations. Say plainly when the sources do not answer it.
- Then write a short overview and organise the rest by theme under "## " headings, as bullet points.
- When there is more than one source, add "## Where sources agree" and "## Where sources disagree", citing each side. If they do not disagree on anything, say so.
- Do not add facts that are not in the notes.

Question: Which G-Wagon years are the best and the worst to buy, and why?

Sources: 2

### Best & Worst G-Wagon Years: Reliability, Interiors & Engines Ranked!
(Alliance Motorworks, duration 18:04)
Notes:
- The video will provide a year-by-year breakdown of the legendary W463 platform to help viewers choose the best G-Wagon model year [0:00]
- The host, Adam, is joined by Joe from Alliance Autocare, a G-Wagon specialist, to discuss the best and worst G-Wagon years to buy [0:16]
- The video features three trucks: a 2000 G500, a 2012 G55 AMG, and a 2015 G550, which will be compared in terms of engine options and interior [0:42]
- The 2000 G500 has a legendary M113 V8 engine, known for its reliability and durability, and is often referred to as the "Land Cruiser killer" [1:00]
- The M113 V8 engine is a single overhead cam motor with timing chains, two spark plugs per cylinder, and produces 300 horsepower and 300 ft-lb of torque [1:15]
- The engine is made of aluminum, is super light, and has parts that are cheap and widely available, making it a "Global Motor" [1:31]
- The 2000 G500 has the original interior, known as the first-gen 463 interior, which features a lot of wood, mechanical switches, and a shifter in the middle [2:03]
- The interior has a "definite sense of occasion" and feels rich, tactile, and special, with a great driving experience and commanding view [2:32]
- The G-Wagon's driving experience is similar across different model years, with the platform remaining virtually unchanged from 1979 to 2018 [3:12]
- The 2000 G500 has 171,000 miles on it, but the leather quality is still excellent, with no rips, tears, or cracks, demonstrating Mercedes' high-quality leather [3:41]
- The G55 AMG was introduced in 2003 as a naturally aspirated model and later became supercharged in 2005, producing 491 horsepower [4:14]
- The supercharged G55 AMG uses a 5-speed automatic transmission and is known for being robust and reliable, but may drink a little oil as it ages [4:43]
- The G55 AMG has a 5,000-mile service interval and is relatively easy to maintain, despite drinking some oil, with this particular truck consuming a quart and a half between oil changes [5:00]
- The door panel on the G55 AMG is physically wider, with door switches and seat switches on the door, making the cabin feel a little snugger [5:45]
- The G55 AMG was available with the M113 engine until 2012, and buyers had two options: the G500 and the G55 AMG [5:59]
- The 2012 G-Wagon has an updated dash with a new instrument cluster and tech, including a command system and a screen [6:12]
- The designo seats in the 2012 G-Wagon are fantastic and were carried through to 2018 with the same seat controls, pneumatic pumps, and stitching [6:42]
- Mercedes' leather quality is unmatched, with no signs of rips, stains, tears, or fading in the leather of a 2012 G-Wagon with 128,000 miles [6:59]
- The G500 has a similar steering wheel to the G550, with slight updates and buttons on the steering wheel [7:14]
- An aftermarket head unit can be installed in any G-Wagon to provide hands-free phone options and media playing, with Apple CarPlay and Android audio capabilities [7:28]
- Adding a backup camera and upgrading the head unit can make an old G-Wagon look and feel new [7:38]
- To make an old G-Wagon look new, three things can be done: upgrade the wheels and tires, upgrade the head unit, and upgrade the suspension [8:02]
- The G500 (2002-2010) is recommended for first-time G-Wagon buyers on a budget, as it represents the best value on the market [8:17]
- The G55 is recommended for those who want to build a high-performance off-road platform with a lot of power [8:34]
- The G55 is more maintenance-intensive than the G500, but it's a blast to drive [9:01]
- The interior of the 2012-2018 G-Wagons is virtually identical, making it difficult to tell the difference between models [9:14]
- The 2015 G550 has a M278 dual overhead cam naturally aspirated V8 engine, which represents a big technological leap forward from Mercedes [9:41]
- The M278 engine is reliable, makes the right amount of power, and is suitable for big tasks [10:11]
- The seven-speed automatic transmission in the 2013-2018 G-Wagons is a game-changer in terms of handling and driving [10:26]
- The exterior of the 2013-2018 G-Wagons looks similar, with the same grill and headlights, but with cool little LED strips under the lights [10:50]
- The trucks can be individualized with aftermarket upgrades, such as LEDs and blacked-out lights [11:03]
- The interior of the 2013-2018 G-Wagons has a general style that runs through the model years, with subtle tweaks to the infotainment system and steering wheel [11:28]
- The seats in the 2013-2018 G-Wagons are the same as those introduced in 2010 and are a great design that works well [11:41]
- The 2013‑2015 G‑Wagon models are praised as the “ultimate daily driver,” offering a comfortable ride for everything from date nights to client pickups, making them ideal for everyday use. [14:08]  
- These same 2013‑2015 models are highlighted as the favorite off‑road platform because they have the right technology, are not overly complicated, and “just work” for off‑road builds. [14:23]  
- The 2016‑2018 G‑Wagon introduced a manual driving mode and Auto‑Stop‑Start, but also added a turbocharged 4.0 L “Hot‑V” engine that, while delivering 419 hp and about 1.5 mpg better fuel economy, brings extra complexity and turbo lag compared to the naturally aspirated V8. [12:53] [13:23]  
- The 4.0 L biturbo engine (2016‑2018) produces roughly 60‑70 hp more than the naturally aspirated V8, but the added forced‑induction makes the throttle “more twitchy” and less suited for off‑road driving. [16:20]  
- The 2016‑2018 G‑63 variant steps up to a 5.1 L twin‑turbo V8 with 560 hp, offering high performance but further increasing complexity, auxiliary cooling, and limiting off‑road modification options. [13:36]  
- The last year of the naturally aspirated V8 was 2015, meaning 2013‑2015 models retain a simpler engine layout with fewer auxiliary coolers, giving owners more freedom for off‑road bumpers and other modifications. [15:23]  
- Because the naturally aspirated engine lacks turbochargers, it provides “no turbo lag,” smoother low‑end response, and higher reliability, making it the preferred choice for serious off‑road enthusiasts. [16:20]  
- The 2016‑2018 turbo models are considered less reliable due to the added complexity of forced induction and extra cooling systems, which can be a drawback for buyers prioritizing durability. [16:36]  
- For buyers on a tighter budget seeking the best value‑for‑money, the early‑2000s G‑500 (MBUSA) is recommended as an economical option that still delivers solid performance. [17:01]
